name: Claude model and effort level in Claude Code
takeaway: Explains the two independent dials: model choice and effort level (low/medium/high/max). Headline figure - on the same prompt, high effort generates roughly 7x more tokens than low. Guidance is to leave effort at default and only move it for a specific reason.
whatToDo: Reference. Action: set a house default - mid-tier model at medium for routine build work, top model at high/max reserved for architecture, migrations and debugging - and write it into team practice.
notes: Directly controls cost-per-task on client delivery. Knowing high effort is ~7x the tokens lets you set sensible house defaults instead of burning max effort on boilerplate.
Model line-ups churn fast; re-check the page before quoting specific model names to a client. The 7x figure and the effort ladder were consistent across fetches.
adminNote: House default set from this: mid-tier model at medium for routine build work, top model at high only for architecture and debugging.

name: ClaudeDevs (@ClaudeDevs)
takeaway: Confirmed official Anthropic X account for developers building with Claude - changelogs, API updates, Claude Code releases, tips, webinars and community news. Announced by @claudeai on 16 April 2026 and described by Anthropic's Thariq as the official channel for Claude Code and Claude platform updates.
whatToDo: Nothing to build - follow it, or pipe it into a Foundry digest if you would rather not open X.
notes: If you build with Claude Code and MCP inside Foundry, this is the primary first-party feed for breaking changes, new agent features and deprecations that could break internal tooling.

UNVERIFIED by direct fetch - x.com blocks automated fetching, so bio, follower count and recent posts were not read. Official status verified indirectly via the @claudeai announcement post and Anthropic staff. Signal is decent but it is still a marketing-adjacent channel; the docs changelog remains the authoritative source for breaking changes.

name: Expo (@expo)
takeaway: Official X account for Expo, the open-source framework and hosted platform for building universal native apps with React (iOS, Android, web). Behind Expo SDK, EAS Build/Submit/Update and expo-router. Feed carries SDK releases and changelogs.
whatToDo: Nothing to build. Follow the release feed.
notes: If you build client mobile apps at all, Expo is the default React Native toolchain and its SDK cadence dictates upgrade and maintenance work on every app you ship.

UNVERIFIED - x.com blocks automated fetching, so bio and recent posts were not read; identity confirmed by search. For uptime and incident signal, which matters more for Foundry monitoring, follow @expo_status instead - @expo is the marketing feed.
cost: Free. Expo framework is MIT; EAS cloud services priced separately.
adminNote: Follow @expo_status for incidents — @expo itself is the marketing feed.

name: Figma Make kits
takeaway: Reusable bundles you attach to a Figma Make file so AI-generated prototypes come out in your product's actual look and behaviour. A kit holds npm packages (your real component library), variables and styles from published Figma libraries, and markdown guidelines. Publish per org, admins can approve and default them.
whatToDo: Reference. Action: publish one Make kit per retained client (their npm component package + published library variables + guidelines.md) and treat the kit as a delivery artefact alongside the Foundry design system.
notes: This is how you make Figma Make output land in a client's actual design system, which is exactly the gap between your Figma work and your build output.

Two stated gotchas: Make kits do not fully extract design tokens - variables get flattened into a global CSS file with raw values, so semantic token naming does not survive. A kit is a downstream consumer of Foundry's token JSON, not a replacement. Importing asset-heavy libraries can take minutes. Needs Full seats, so cheap-seat freelancers cannot use it.
cost: Included in paid Figma. Requires Full seats.
adminNote: Publish one kit per retained client and treat it as a delivery artefact.

name: Steering Claude Code: skills, hooks, rules, subagents
takeaway: Anthropic's guide to the seven ways to customise Claude Code and when to use each: CLAUDE.md, path-scoped rules, skills, subagents, hooks, output styles, --system-prompt. Organising principle is the trade-off between context cost and authority.
whatToDo: Reference. Action: audit the .claude/ setup for Foundry and client repos - move anything living in a bloated CLAUDE.md into path-scoped rules or on-demand skills.
notes: You already run skills and MCP against Foundry - this is the canonical guide to structuring them so agent behaviour is repeatable across client projects.
Decision framework, not a syntax reference. For exact file formats you still need the docs site. The mapping to Foundry workflows is your work, not the post's.
adminNote: Action: audit the .claude/ setup for Foundry and client repos against the seven mechanisms.

name: designengineer.tools
takeaway: Single-page curated list of ~150 tools across ~20 categories scoped specifically to web design engineers: inspiration, AI coding assistants, component libraries, colour utilities, shader editors, motion, 3D. Curated by James Warner.
whatToDo: Nothing to build publicly. If you want a version, it belongs as a Foundry wiki page of the studio's own vetted tools so the knowledge survives the site.
notes: The most on-target directory of the batch - scoped precisely to the discipline you practise, so it works as a one-sitting audit of gaps in the studio toolchain.

No update date means entries in the fast-moving AI-coding category may already be stale, and a one-person link list can go unmaintained without warning. Read it once, diff against your current stack, record adoptions in Foundry.
adminNote: Read once, diff against the studio stack, record adoptions in the Foundry wiki.

name: iOS 27 Media Intelligence framework (Anton Gubarenko)
takeaway: Technical write-up of Apple's new Media Intelligence framework in iOS 27 - an on-device layer above Vision that reasons about relationships across a whole media collection rather than single images. Two main pieces: FaceGroupAnalyzer (detect faces, persist results, cluster into person groups) and VideoAnalyzer (KeyFrameAnalysisRequest for representative frames, HighlightAnalysisRequest for interesting segments).
whatToDo: Reference article. The build question is whether to use the framework in a client app - and Apple's on-device API is obviously cheaper than rolling your own clustering pipeline.
notes: Directly useful only if you are building an iOS app with photo or video libraries, but exactly the kind of new-API signal to have on file when a client asks for 'AI photo features' in a mobile brief.

Constraints worth knowing before scoping: it needs a writable working directory, asset IDs must stay stable across launches, all processing is local (a privacy selling point for pitches), analysis should be kept off the MainActor, and there is no Simulator support - physical device testing is mandatory, which affects QA estimates. Key limitation: numeric confidence scores for face grouping are not publicly exposed, so an app can group appearances but cannot verify identity. Do not let a client spec 'identify this person' on top of it.

name: Leon Lin - 'How To Actually Design With AI'
takeaway: An X post or thread titled 'How To Actually Design With AI' by Leon Lin, a designer who posts AI-design workflow breakdowns and tool comparisons. Opinion and tutorial content on process, not a product.
whatToDo: Written content. The only build would be turning its ideas into an internal process doc - short, if the thread turns out to be any good.
notes: Practitioner write-ups on AI design workflow are useful raw material if you want to codify a repeatable AI-assisted design process into a Foundry starter or internal playbook.

UNVERIFIED and the weakest item of the batch. Fetch blocked; only the title and author are confirmed. Do not treat the summary as content-verified. The author writes engagement-oriented design-Twitter content - inspiration, not authority. Multiple unrelated people share the name.

name: Thariq (@trq212) post
takeaway: A single post by Thariq, who works at Anthropic on Claude Code and regularly posts practical Claude Code guidance. The post body could not be retrieved.
whatToDo: Open it manually in a browser. Follow the account rather than treating single posts as reference material.
notes: The account is consistently high-signal on Claude Code practice, directly applicable to how you run agent-assisted delivery. This individual post's value is unassessable.

UNVERIFIED - fetch blocked on both x.com and twitter.com; the date is inference from tweet ID, not fact. Nothing here should be quoted as the post's content. Separately verified from search: the same account posted in early August 2026 that ~80% of the Claude Code system prompt was removed for the newest models, with a blog write-up - that is probably the more useful post if you are chasing current guidance.

name: Vercel Open Source Program
takeaway: Sponsorship programme giving selected open-source projects $3,600 in Vercel credits over 12 months, plus an OSS Starter Pack of third-party credits and priority guidance from Vercel staff. Requires an actively maintained OSS project hosted on Vercel, demonstrable impact, and a published Code of Conduct.
whatToDo: Nothing to build. The actual work is deciding whether any Gitwork tooling is worth extracting and maintaining in public.
notes: Only useful if you open-source something real - a design-system starter, a Foundry SDK, a component library. Foundry itself is commercial and would not qualify.

Be sceptical about the economics: ~$300/month of credit, and 'credits exclusively for open source work' means you cannot quietly offset client hosting. The Code of Conduct and actively-maintained bars create an ongoing obligation. 'Reopen in August' may mean now - worth re-checking. Funded OSS companies get redirected to the separate Startups Program.
cost: Free to the recipient - $3,600 Vercel credit over 12 months plus partner credits.
adminNote: $3,600 of credit, but it creates a maintenance obligation. Only worth it if we open-source something real.

name: 'Create an AI Inbox Manager' PDF (Dupple)
takeaway: ~9-page tutorial PDF from Dupple's 'AI Academy' on building an automated inbox assistant in Make plus GPT-4o-mini: email trigger, keyword filters, prompt mapping, response templates with sentiment handling, escalation to a human. Ends with a course upsell.
whatToDo: An enquiry-triage-and-draft-reply flow off the agency inbox is a genuine weekend job - but build it against your own stack, not by following this PDF.
notes: The Make-plus-GPT inbox triage pattern is mildly useful as inspiration for automating agency enquiry handling, but the content is beginner-level and adds nothing you could not build in Foundry.
Marketing content with a course upsell, not a tool. The URL is a tracked bucket link that could rot at any time - save the takeaway, not the link.

name: Apple Metal
takeaway: Apple's landing page for Metal, its low-overhead GPU graphics and compute API across iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple TV and Vision Pro, with a shading language, profiling tools and sub-frameworks (MetalFX, MPS, MPS Graph).
whatToDo: Apple's first-party GPU API. Nothing to build.
notes: A design-and-build agency shipping websites, apps and design systems will realistically never write Metal code - you would only meet it indirectly via a game engine, a WebGPU/Three.js layer or someone else's native SDK.
Reference page for engine and graphics engineers, not an agency tool. Probably landed on the list from a tangent rather than delivery work. Bookmark-worthy at most.

name: beacon (angaziz)
takeaway: One-person prototype companion device on a Waveshare ESP32-S3 AMOLED board - five screens showing Claude/Codex usage, markets, weather and a coding tool-approval interface, driven over Bluetooth by a macOS hub app.
whatToDo: Not worth adopting. If the ambient-status idea appeals, a Foundry web dashboard on a cheap wall tablet gets 90% of the value for a fraction of the effort.
notes: The only reusable idea is the ambient display - a small always-on screen showing live status, which maps loosely onto Foundry's uptime monitors.
6 stars, 0 forks, single author, explicitly an early prototype. Needs specific hardware and a Mac to run at all. Inspiration only - do not depend on it.
cost: Free / MIT. Needs specific hardware and a Mac.

name: chat-stick (Steve Ruiz)
takeaway: Personal hardware project by Steve Ruiz of tldraw - a handheld push-to-talk voice interface for LLMs on ESP32-S3 devices, C++ firmware talking to Gemini Live via a Cloudflare Worker relay.
whatToDo: Nothing to build - it is a device. The software half is a weekend to reproduce if you ever need it, and reading this repo is cheaper.
notes: Hobby hardware with no bearing on client sites, apps or design systems. The one transferable part is the Worker relay pattern for streaming realtime voice with server-side tool calls.

Worth a look mainly for who wrote it - Ruiz's code is usually worth reading for taste and structure. Needs ESP32-S3 hardware and a Gemini API key to do anything. Clearly a personal experiment, shipped as-is.
cost: Free / MIT. Needs ESP32-S3 hardware and a Gemini API key.

name: go2rtc issue #1738
takeaway: A support question (not a bug) on go2rtc, AlexxIT's MIT-licensed Go camera streaming app (13.1k stars) that ingests RTSP/ONVIF and republishes as WebRTC/HLS/RTSP/RTMP. A user reports a Hikvision doorbell stream working in browsers but never loading inside the Home Assistant iOS app.
whatToDo: go2rtc solves camera protocol translation and codec negotiation properly and for free. Writing your own RTSP-to-WebRTC bridge is a multi-month specialist job with no agency upside.
notes: Only relevant if a client project involves embedding live camera or WebRTC video in a mobile webview. The general lesson is worth filing: WebRTC that works in Safari can still fail inside an app webview, and codec negotiation is usually why.

GitHub did not return the comment thread to the fetch, so it is unknown whether anyone replied or a workaround exists - do not assume it is unanswered. Nothing here indicates a defect in go2rtc itself.
cost: N/A - go2rtc itself is free / MIT

name: macapp.supply
takeaway: Hand-curated directory of well-designed macOS apps - 'a curated shelf of beautifully designed macOS apps' - covering indie tools, utilities and craft-led software. Curated by Solt Wagner. Aimed at Mac users, not builders.
whatToDo: The software is trivial - a list, categories, a submission form and a Stripe link. The only asset is curation and audience, neither of which you acquire by cloning it.
notes: A consumer software shelf - occasionally useful for spotting a nicely made Mac utility for the studio, and decent inspiration for how a small directory should look, but it touches nothing in client delivery or Foundry.

Two things worth taking rather than using: the $100 for 30 days featured-listing model is a clean example of monetising a directory without paywalling it, and the submission form's field spec (60-char short description, 6000-char long, 1200x630 cover, icon, up to 10 gallery images, optional video) is ready-made if you ever build a showcase or client-portfolio directory in Foundry. Single-curator dependency: if the curator stops, the site stops.
cost: Free to browse. $100 for a 30-day featured listing if you ever want to place an app there.

name: Macfolio
takeaway: Curated discovery site for the Mac ecosystem - software, hardware, workspace setups, books, videos - with a newsletter archive and blog. Same operator as Toolfolio.
whatToDo: Nothing to build. It is a content play whose only asset is editorial taste and an audience, neither transferable.
notes: Consumer gear and app curation. Occasionally useful for kitting out the studio, but touches nothing in your build, design-system or Foundry workflow.
One-person side project in a crowded genre (Setapp, MacStories, Uses This). No moat beyond curation. Bookmark for hardware research; not worth strategic attention.

name: Toolfolio
takeaway: General-purpose tool discovery directory spanning 20+ categories plus 8 ecosystem libraries (YC, Framer, Figma, Apple, Shopify, Notion, Webflow, Chrome) and curated collections.
whatToDo: Building another tool directory is pure content labour with no defensibility - saturated, SEO-dependent, and it would compete with billable work.
notes: Broad consumer-grade listings are too shallow to inform agency tooling decisions. The Figma and Framer library pages are the only slices with any pull.

Read as a solo-operator SEO/affiliate directory, not a product. Depth is a sentence or two per tool, and inclusion likely reflects submissions and affiliate availability rather than testing - so presence or absence is not a quality signal. One genuinely useful angle: getting Foundry listed is cheap or free and could send some qualified traffic.

name: @bateshkaaa post
takeaway: A single X post by the account @bateshkaaa. Neither the account's identity nor the post's content could be established.
whatToDo: Nothing to build; there is no identified product behind this link.
notes: Nothing verifiable to act on - an unattributed single post is not something to plan around.

UNVERIFIED - fetch blocked by x.com. Searches for the handle and the exact status ID returned zero relevant results; several similar 'Bates' handles exist and none is a match, so no assumption was made. The post content was deliberately not guessed. If you want this assessed, paste the post text or a screenshot, or open it while logged in.

name: Metal Performance Shaders docs
takeaway: Apple's API reference for MPS, a framework of pre-built GPU compute and graphics kernels hand-tuned per GPU family - image filtering, matrix and linear algebra, neural network inference on Apple devices.
whatToDo: Vendor framework documentation. Nothing to build.
notes: Deep native GPU kernel territory with no bearing on websites, web apps, design systems or Foundry.
Even less agency-relevant than the Metal overview - this is the sub-framework. Honestly does not belong on an agency tools list. The page is JS-rendered so only the abstract was readable.

name: posts.design
takeaway: A hand-picked wall of social post design — 378 captures of product updates, announcements and launches from X, browsable by recency or by brand, each keeping its creator, platform and original link. Run by one curator (@baseddesigner) whose stated filter is what is worth stealing rather than what spreads.
whatToDo: Reference, not a dependency. Open it when designing a launch or announcement post for a client or for Gitwork, take the structure and the hierarchy, and leave the styling behind. Anything genuinely good gets screenshotted into the Foundry wiki rather than relied on staying up.
notes: Narrow but real: announcement and launch post design is a surface we produce for nearly every client, and there is no decent reference for it beyond scrolling a feed. It is inspiration only — no product, no export, no API, nothing to install.

Same IP caution as Flaude and Refero Styles. These are other companies' posts and trade dress. Fine as internal reference; a problem if a layout or a line of copy survives into a client deliverable, so treat it as structure-only input.

One person, no company, free by choice with tips — assume it can disappear. /pricing and /submit both returned 500 when requested directly, so free-forever is the curator's current position rather than a commitment, and takedowns are handled by DM.
cost: Free. No ads and no paywall; the curator asks for voluntary tips.

name: The Component Gallery
takeaway: 60 interface components cross-referenced against 95 published design systems, with 2,671 concrete examples — so for any component you can read how Carbon, Polaris, Material and 90 others named it, structured it and what states they defined. Also lists the design systems themselves.
whatToDo: Reference before naming or specifying a component. Action: when a client design system needs a component we have not built before, open its page here first and steal the naming and the state list rather than inventing them.
notes: The value is settling arguments cheaply: 'is it a Toast or a Snackbar, and does it need a dismiss action' becomes a five-second lookup across 95 systems instead of a meeting.
It is a reference index, not code — every example links out to someone else's documentation, so nothing here ships.
Maintained by one person (Iain Bean) and up to date at the time of adding. Worth screenshotting anything a client design system depends on.

name: Easing Functions Cheat Sheet
takeaway: Every standard easing curve — the ease-in/out/inOut families plus back, elastic and bounce — animated side by side with its graph, its cubic-bezier CSS value and its maths, so you can pick by watching rather than by name.
whatToDo: Reference during motion work. Action: when a transition feels wrong, open this, find the curve that matches the intent, and paste the cubic-bezier value rather than nudging numbers.
notes: The reason to keep it to hand: naming is the problem in motion work — 'make it snappier' is unactionable, 'easeOutBack, 400ms' is a spec. This turns taste into a value you can put in a PR.
Copy the cubic-bezier values, not the site's source. The page code is GPL-3.0, which would be a licensing problem in a client repo; the curves themselves are just numbers.
Static reference, no dependency, nothing to break.
cost: Free. The site's own code is GPL-3.0.

name: Design Spells
takeaway: A catalogue of individual delightful details captured from shipped products — easter eggs, transitions, confetti, Dynamic Island tricks, 404s — each tagged by type and platform (Mobile, Desktop, Interaction, Animation, Skeuomorphic). One detail per entry, not whole screens.
whatToDo: Reference when a build needs one memorable moment. Action: pick a single spell to implement on the next Gitwork or client site rather than scattering effects across it.
notes: Useful precisely because it is granular: the entries are things a developer can implement in an afternoon, unlike a full-page inspiration shot that implies a redesign.
Run by two people (Chester and Duncan) with a newsletter attached — assume it can go quiet. Capture anything worth reusing rather than linking to it from internal docs.
Every entry is another product's craft. Take the idea and rebuild it; do not copy assets.
cost: Free. Newsletter and sponsor slots; no paywall.

name: 60fps.design
takeaway: 2,024 screen recordings of interaction and animation detail from 475 best-in-class iOS and web apps, plus 77 app sites, 25 motion studies and a handful of code snippets. Recordings rather than stills, and it exposes an MCP endpoint so an agent can query the collection.
whatToDo: Reference for motion specs. Action: when specifying a transition for a client build, find the closest recording here and attach it to the ticket — a video beats an adjective.
notes: The MCP endpoint is the interesting part and the reason this is worth knowing over the other inspiration sites: an agent implementing an interaction can pull real reference instead of guessing at timings.
No pricing page exists, so 'free' is the current state rather than a commitment — the collection may gate later.
Recordings of other companies' products. Fine as a motion spec, not as an asset source.
cost: Free to browse. No pricing page published.

name: Recent (formerly Godly)
takeaway: Daily curation of exceptional websites, split into browsable sections for Websites, OG Images, App Screenshots, App Icons, Resources, Tools, Skills and Jobs, filtered by discipline (Interface, Branding, Typography, Motion, Editorial, Packaging). godly.website now redirects here.
whatToDo: Reference at the start of a site project. Action: use the OG Images and App Icons sections specifically — those are the two assets we produce for every client and the two with the least reference material elsewhere.
notes: The OG image and app icon sections are the genuinely differentiated bit. General website inspiration is oversupplied; a curated wall of 379 OG images is not.
Note the redirect: anything in our notes pointing at godly.website is now Recent, so the old bookmark is stale rather than dead.
3,498 members at the time of adding, with signups climbing fast — an early-stage curation site, so screenshot what matters.
cost: Free to browse; account for saving. No pricing page published.

name: Saaspo
takeaway: 3,097 SaaS pages broken down into 716 individual sections, plus 379 OG images and 46 templates, filterable so you can look at pricing sections or testimonial blocks in isolation rather than whole homepages.
whatToDo: Reference when specifying a marketing site. Action: pull the relevant section type (pricing, feature grid, social proof) before writing the wireframe, so the structure argument happens against 20 shipped examples.
notes: Section-level filtering is what separates it from Awwwards-style galleries: our work is usually 'this pricing table is not converting', not 'redesign everything', and this indexes at that granularity.
Narrow to SaaS, which covers a good share of our client base and none of the rest.
Sponsor-funded with no pricing page — free today, no commitment. Other companies' pages, so structure-only input as ever.
cost: Free to browse; funded by sponsor slots. No pricing page (returns 404).

name: Cosmos
takeaway: Visual reference tool where you build private connected collections and search across everything by colour or by visual similarity rather than by tag. Includes an AI-content filter with show, blur and hide settings, which no other reference library here offers.
whatToDo: Reference management. Action: trial it against GatherOS for holding client mood boards, and turn the AI filter to hide when collecting craft references.
notes: Search by colour and by visual similarity is the actual feature. Finding 'the reference with that exact green' across a year of saves is the thing tag-based tools cannot do.

The AI-content toggle matters more than it sounds: an inspiration library quietly filling with generated images is worthless for craft reference, and this is the only one here that lets you exclude it.
Pricing unverified — /pricing, /about and the help centre all render client-side and returned nothing readable, so assume a paid tier exists and check in-app before the team standardises on it.
cost: Free to join. Paid tiers are not published on any page we could read — the pricing route renders nothing without JavaScript.

name: UNCUT.wtf
takeaway: 163 contemporary typefaces, all free for commercial use, filtered by classification — 66 sans, 47 display, 27 serif, 23 monospace. Curated for current type rather than comprehensive, which is why the hit rate is high.
whatToDo: Source fonts here before proposing a licensed family. Action: on the next brand or site project, shortlist from UNCUT first and check each font's own licence file before it reaches a client deliverable.
notes: Directly saves client budget: a display face with real personality at no licence cost, and no per-domain webfont renewal to explain to a client three years later.

'Free for commercial use' is the catalogue's framing, but each typeface carries its own licence from its own designer. Read the individual licence before shipping — some restrict webfont use or redistribution even when the desktop file is free.
One curator, running since 2021. The fonts are downloaded files, so the catalogue disappearing costs us nothing already in a project.
cost: Free for commercial use. All fonts remain copyright of their respective creators.

name: Fontshare
takeaway: 100 font families from the Indian Type Foundry, free for personal and commercial use, with variable versions, OpenType feature listings and a web API for serving them. Professionally drawn families rather than a mixed catalogue — Satoshi, Switzer and General Sans come from here.
whatToDo: First stop for a free workhorse sans or serif. Action: use the API's licence field to confirm each family before it ships, and self-host the files rather than hotlinking their CDN on a client site.
notes: The quality gap against most free catalogues is the point: these are foundry-drawn families with proper weights and OpenType features, so they hold up as a client's primary typeface rather than only as display type.

The licence page itself is JavaScript-only and did not render for us, so we have confirmed the licence type (itf_ffl) from their API but not read the terms. Read them before a client site depends on it.
One foundry behind all 100 families, which cuts both ways — consistent quality, single point of failure. Self-host the woff2 files in the repo.
cost: Free. Every family in their API carries license_type "itf_ffl" — the ITF Free Font Licence.

name: skills.sh
takeaway: Leaderboard and installer for agent skills — `npx skills add owner/repo` pulls a skill into your agent, and the directory ranks skills by anonymous install telemetry from that CLI. Supports packs, which bundle public and private skills behind one install command. The CLI is open source at vercel-labs/skills.
whatToDo: Action: publish the Foundry starters worth sharing as a skills pack, and check the leaderboard before writing a skill from scratch — install counts are a better signal of what actually works than a README.
notes: Packs are the directly useful bit for us: a private pack of Gitwork skills installed with one command on every machine and in every client repo, instead of copying .claude directories by hand.

The ranking is install telemetry, not review — popular is not the same as good, and a skill that installs into an agent gets to run instructions on our machines. Read any skill's source before adding it.
Vercel Labs project, so treat it as an experiment with a company behind it rather than a supported product.

name: Velvetyne Type Foundry
takeaway: A libre type foundry, not a catalogue — French collective releasing experimental typefaces under free licences, with the sources on GitLab, an In Use section showing where each face has shipped, and workshops and writing about the politics of type.
whatToDo: Source display type here when a brand needs a face with a point of view. Action: check each family's licence file on GitLab (they vary) before it ships, and use the In Use section to see how a face behaves at real sizes.
notes: Different job from Fontshare and UNCUT: these are experimental, opinionated faces — the ones that make a brand look like it was designed rather than configured.
Sources on GitLab means a face can be modified for a client, which almost no commercial licence allows. That is a real capability if a brand needs a bespoke ligature or a missing glyph.
Licences vary per family and are not uniform across the foundry, so read the specific one. A collective rather than a company — pace of updates follows volunteers.

name: Open Foundry
takeaway: A decade-old curated showcase of open-source typefaces — Archivo, Work Sans, Aileron, Bluu Next, Terminal Grotesque and others — presented with their makers and specimen views rather than as a download grid.
whatToDo: Use it to shortlist an open-source workhorse with a specimen you can actually judge. Action: pair it with Fontshare and UNCUT as the three free-type sources, and record which one a client's face came from in their brand doc.
notes: Curation is the value — it is a small set chosen for quality, which is the opposite of Google Fonts' thousands and much faster to decide from.
Open-source licences, so the same families can be self-hosted and modified without a webfont subscription to renew.
It showcases rather than hosts, so downloads land you on each project's own repo where the licence lives. Read it there.

name: Open Source Alternative To
takeaway: 505 open-source alternatives to proprietary products, each listed against the product it replaces with its GitHub star count and category — Godot for Unity, and equivalents across analytics, CRM, forms, storage and design.
whatToDo: Open it when a client baulks at a SaaS line item or needs data on their own infrastructure. Action: check it before proposing a paid tool in a scope of work, so the open alternative is a considered choice rather than an oversight.
notes: Directly useful in proposals: 'the open-source equivalent is X, self-hosted, and here is what it costs to run' is a stronger position than only quoting the SaaS.
Star counts are the only quality signal it carries — popularity is not maintenance. Check commit recency and licence on anything before recommending it to a client.
Self-hosting moves cost from a subscription to our time. Say that plainly when proposing one, or it lands as a saving that later becomes a support burden.

name: awesome-ios-design-md
takeaway: Reverse-engineered design systems for 200 real apps as plain markdown — exact brand hexes, full type ramps, component states, spacing grids, motion curves and haptics — in four flavours each: framework-neutral, SwiftUI, Expo and Jetpack Compose. Hand one to a coding agent and it stops inventing the styling. MIT, by Muhammed Eliwat.
whatToDo: Already done: all 200 apps and 800 specs are vendored into this site under /design-md, with the licence alongside, so they survive the repo going quiet. Action: on the next app build, open the closest app's spec and take the structure — the spacing grid, the motion curves, the component states — not the brand colours.
notes: The specs are unusually good: not "use a card with a shadow" but the actual hex, the actual type weight ladder, the actual spring curve and haptic. That is the difference between an agent producing something plausible and something that looks native.

The IP line matters more here than anywhere else on this site. These are other companies' trade dress. Lifting Bumble's yellow and hexagons into a client's dating app is not inspiration, and the proprietary typefaces named throughout — Brando, Uber Move, Airbnb Cereal, Spotify Mix — must be licensed separately. Take the mechanics; leave the identity.
One maintainer, and the value is entirely in the documents rather than in any service, which is exactly why they are copied into our repo rather than linked.
cost: Free. MIT licence on the documents; the brands they describe are not licensed to anyone.

name: Spectr gallery
takeaway: Live browser-rendered previews of every screen in the 200 apps that awesome-ios-design-md documents, so you can see the interface a spec describes before reading 25KB of markdown. The same outfit sells generating a DESIGN.md from your own screen recording.
whatToDo: Use it as the visual index to the specs on /design-md — find the screen, then take the spec. Action: when a client references "something like the Spotify now-playing screen", open it here on the call rather than describing it.
notes: The pairing is the point: the gallery shows what a screen looks like, the spec says why. Neither is much use to an agent without the other.

Their generate-from-a-recording product is the interesting bit for us — a client's existing app turned into a spec our agents can build against. Unpriced here, so treat it as worth a look rather than a plan.
cost: Gallery is free to browse. Generating your own spec from a recording is their paid product; figures not checked.

name: Frontpages
takeaway: A curated gallery of landing page front pages — hero sections from across the web, searchable by category and company, updated weekly. Its author pitches it as a free version of Mobbin for the web rather than for apps.
whatToDo: Reference at the start of a marketing site. Action: pull ten hero sections in the client's category before wireframing, so the structure argument happens against shipped examples rather than opinions.
notes: Narrower and more useful than a general inspiration gallery: it indexes the one section every client argues about most, and it is free where Mobbin's web coverage is behind $10/month.
Hero sections only, so it complements Saaspo's section-level index rather than replacing it.
Other companies' pages. Structure and hierarchy are the input; the styling is theirs.
cost: Free. Optional email subscription for the weekly update.

name: IP as Logo library
takeaway: The companion gallery to the IP as Logo skill already in the starter library: a searchable wall of finished mascots made with it, each downloadable as its original PNG, with favourites and six UI languages. The skill's README states every logo is free for commercial use. Built as a Supabase and Cloudflare R2 front end, so it is a real library rather than a screenshot of one.
whatToDo: Source. Action: pull two or three mascots as stand-in brand marks for Foundry pitch decks and early prototypes rather than generating from scratch, and run the skill itself (`npx skills@latest add s1dashu/ip-as-logo-skill`) when a client needs something of their own.
notes: Not a client identity. Every visitor can download the same mascots, so treat this as placeholder and side-project material — the skill is what produces something a client can own.
PNG only: the download is the original raster, with no SVG, so anything that needs to scale or recolour has to be redrawn.
The commercial-use grant is a line in the GitHub README (MIT, s1dashu, 2026), not a licence file on the site itself. Keep a copy of that wording if a logo ever ends up in front of a client.
Single maintainer, a client-side app on Supabase with the publishable key in the bundle and assets on cdn.ipaslogo.com. Fine for what it is; download anything we rely on rather than hotlinking it.

name: Claude Academy
takeaway: Anthropic's own course catalogue: 289 courses, tutorials and use cases in one filterable list. The ones that matter to us are Claude Code 101 (12 lessons on what it is and the core workflows), Claude Code in Action (9 lessons on long hands-off sessions — plan mode, steering compaction, the rewind menu, autonomous loops, verification), Introduction to agent skills (6 lessons from a first skill to team distribution), Claude subagents (4 lessons on orchestrating them deterministically), Introduction to MCP, Introduction to Claude Cowork (14 lessons) and Building with the Claude API (67 lessons covering tool use, RAG, agents and production patterns).
whatToDo: Training. Action: everyone does Claude Code in Action and Introduction to agent skills — they are an hour each and they cover exactly the things people are currently guessing at, from compaction to skill distribution. Then Building with the Claude API for whoever is next on an agent build.
notes: This is the answer to most of the "how do I make it stop doing that" questions: plan mode, directing compaction so a summary keeps what matters, rewinding a session, when to hand over to a loop. All of it documented by the people who built it rather than inferred from a thread.
Courses open without an account — "Start course" works, and signing in only saves progress and completion badges. Free, © 2026 Anthropic PBC, and the catalogue is filterable by product.

Most of the 289 entries are not for us: the AI Fluency family (builders, educators, nonprofits, small businesses, students, pK–12) and the Bedrock and Vertex courses are 65-plus lessons each. Filter to the Claude Code and skills material and ignore the rest until there is a reason.
adminNote: Start here. Everything else on this site assumes you already know what Claude Code can do.
